### Cellulitis (Non-Purulent SSTI)
- Spreading erythema, warmth, edema, tenderness without drainable collection
- Poorly defined borders, often unilateral
- Entry point: skin break, wound, tinea pedis, insect bite
- Most common pathogen: Group A Streptococcus (GAS), also Staphylococcus aureus
- Systemic signs: fever, tachycardia, lymphangitis, regional lymphadenopathy

### Cutaneous Abscess (Purulent SSTI)
- Fluctuant, tender, erythematous mass with overlying warmth
- Point tenderness, may have spontaneous drainage
- Most common pathogen: MRSA (prevalence 50-75% in community abscesses in the US)
- Common locations: axilla, groin, perirectal, buttock, face

### Severity Classification (IDSA)
| Class | Description | Management |
|---|---|---|
| Mild | No systemic signs, immunocompetent | Outpatient oral antibiotics or I&D alone |
| Moderate | Systemic signs (fever, tachycardia, WBC >12 or <4) OR immunocompromised OR failed outpatient therapy | IV antibiotics, observation or admit |
| Severe | Failed IV antibiotics, sepsis, deep space infection, necrotizing fasciitis | Surgical consultation, ICU |

### LRINEC Score (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis)
| Parameter | Criteria | Points |
|---|---|---|
| CRP | ≥ 150 mg/L | 4 |
| WBC | 15-25 × 10⁹/L | 1 |
| WBC | > 25 × 10⁹/L | 2 |
| Hemoglobin | 11-13.5 g/dL | 1 |
| Hemoglobin | < 11 g/dL | 2 |
| Sodium | < 135 mEq/L | 2 |
| Creatinine | > 1.6 mg/dL | 2 |
| Glucose | > 180 mg/dL | 1 |

- Score ≥ 6: Intermediate/high risk for necrotizing fasciitis — surgical consultation
- Score ≥ 8: Strongly predictive — proceed to OR
- Sensitivity is imperfect (68-92%); clinical suspicion overrides a low score

tting shoes and socks or slippers to protect your feet when walking. You don't want to walk barefoot, even indoors. And be sure your shoes are smooth inside. A seam or pebble could rub your skin raw. 
 Protecting your feet from heat and cold. Use sunscreen on exposed skin and don't walk barefoot at the beach. In cold weather, wear warm socks instead of warming your feet near a heater or fireplace. 
 Keeping the blood flowing in your feet. Put your feet up when you're sitting. Wiggle your toes and circle your feet throughout the day. Don't wear tight socks. And get plenty of activity that's not too hard on the feet, such as walking. 
 Getting your feet checked at your health care visits. Even if you haven't noticed a problem, it's good to have your health care provider look at your feet. 
 

 When should I see my health care provider about diabetic foot problems? 
 Serious foot problems can develop quickly. See your health care provider right away if you notice: 
 
 A cut, blister, or bruise on your feet that doesn't start to heal in a few days 
 Red, warm, or painful skin on your feet 
 A callus with dried blood inside 
 A foot infection that becomes black and smells bad that could be gangrene 
 
 Remember, controlling your blood sugar and caring for your feet every day are the best steps you can take to prevent serious diabetic foot problems. 

 NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

### Abscess: Incision and Drainage (I&D)
1. Prep with antiseptic (chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine)
2. Local anesthesia: lidocaine 1% with epinephrine (safe on all locations including digits — digital tourniquet epinephrine myth debunked). Field block around the abscess is more effective than direct injection into cavity.
3. Stab incision with #11 blade over point of maximal fluctuance, extending full length of cavity
4. Express purulent material; send culture
5. Break up all loculations with hemostat or finger (critical step)
6. Irrigate cavity with normal saline
7. Packing: traditional iodoform gauze packing OR loop drain (vessel loop through two stab incisions) — loop drain associated with less pain at follow-up and equivalent outcomes
8. Wound check in 48-72 hours for packing removal/replacement

### Antibiotics for Abscess (Post-I&D)
- Small abscess (< 2 cm) in immunocompetent: I&D alone may suffice (IDSA guidelines); however, recent RCTs (Talan 2016, Daum 2017) show adjunctive TMP-SMX improves cure rates
- **TMP-SMX DS (160/800 mg) 1-2 tabs PO BID x 7-10 days** — MRSA coverage
- **Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x 7-10 days** — alternative MRSA coverage
- **Clindamycin 300-450 mg PO TID x 7-10 days** — alternative; check local resistance (inducible resistance up to 20-50%)

### Antibiotics for Cellulitis (Non-Purulent)
- **Mild (outpatient):**
  - Cephalexin 500 mg PO QID x 5-7 days (covers GAS, MSSA)
  - Dicloxacillin 500 mg PO QID x 5-7 days (alternative)
  - If MRSA risk: add TMP-SMX DS 1-2 tabs PO BID or doxycycline 100 mg PO BID
- **Moderate (IV):**
  - Cefazolin 1-2 g IV q8h
  - If MRSA risk: vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h (target AUC/MIC 400-600) or daptomycin 4 mg/kg IV daily

### Discharge Criteria
- Mild cellulitis: immunocompetent, no systemic signs, reliable follow-up
- Abscess after I&D: pain controlled, no surrounding cellulitis/systemic signs, able to return for wound check in 48-72 hours
- Prescribe oral antibiotics, wound care instructions, clear return precautions

### Admission Criteria
- Systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, hypotension)
- Failed outpatient oral antibiotics (progression despite 48-72 hours of therapy)
- Immunocompromised (diabetes, HIV, transplant, chemotherapy)
- Extensive cellulitis requiring IV antibiotics
- Location requiring close monitoring (face, orbit, hand, perineum)
- Concern for necrotizing fasciitis or deep space infection — surgical consultation and admission
- Unable to tolerate oral medications

### Follow-Up
- Wound check 48-72 hours post-I&D
- Cellulitis re-evaluation at 48-72 hours to assess response (erythema should not extend beyond marked borders)
- Return immediately for: increasing pain, expanding erythema beyond marks, fever, systemic symptoms, crepitus, skin color change to dusky/purple

1. **Missing Klebsiella pneumoniae invasive syndrome.** K. pneumoniae liver abscess (especially K1/K2 serotype) metastasizes to eyes (endophthalmitis → blindness) and CNS. Screen diabetic patients with KPLA with ophthalmology exam and neurologic assessment.

2. **Aspirating an echinococcal cyst mistaken for abscess.** Unprotected aspiration of hydatid cyst causes anaphylaxis and peritoneal seeding. If there is any concern for echinococcus (endemic exposure, calcified wall, daughter cysts), obtain Echinococcus serology BEFORE aspiration.

3. **Insufficient antibiotic duration.** Hepatic abscesses require prolonged therapy (4-6 weeks total). Premature discontinuation leads to recurrence. Follow CRP and imaging to guide duration.

4. **Failing to evaluate for underlying GI malignancy.** Cryptogenic pyogenic liver abscess in patients > 50 is associated with occult colorectal cancer. Colonoscopy after acute phase is mandatory.

5. **Not adding a luminal agent after treating amebic abscess.** Metronidazole alone does not eradicate intestinal colonization. Paromomycin is required to prevent relapse. Omission is the most common error in amebic abscess management.

6. **Treating amebic abscess with drainage first.** Unlike pyogenic abscesses, most amebic abscesses respond to metronidazole alone. Drainage is reserved for large (> 10 cm), left-lobe (pericardial rupture risk), or refractory abscesses.

1. **Delaying antibiotics to obtain cultures.** Draw cultures, then immediately administer antibiotics. Never wait for culture results, LP results, or imaging before giving antibiotics in septic shock.

2. **Using qSOFA as a diagnostic tool rather than a screening tool.** A qSOFA < 2 does NOT exclude sepsis. It was designed for bedside prognostication, not diagnosis. Use clinical judgment and SOFA scoring.

3. **Attributing altered mental status to "baseline" in elderly patients.** Acute confusion is an organ dysfunction marker. Assume sepsis until proven otherwise in elderly patients with altered mentation and any infection risk.

4. **Over-resuscitating with crystalloid without reassessing.** Fluid overload worsens outcomes, especially in ARDS. Reassess with POCUS after every 500-1000 mL. Start vasopressors early if MAP remains < 65 despite 1-2 L.

5. **Failing to identify and control the source.** Antibiotics alone will not resolve undrained abscesses, obstructed viscera, or necrotizing infections. Imaging and surgical consultation are part of first-hour management when source is uncertain.

6. **Not considering occult sources in patients with negative initial workup.** Endocarditis, epidural abscess, prosthetic joint infection, and C. difficile colitis may not be apparent on initial evaluation. Broaden the search when cultures are negative and the patient is not improving.

7. **Underdosing vancomycin.** Use actual body weight for the loading dose (25-30 mg/kg). A 100 kg patient needs 2.5-3 g, not the traditional 1 g.

chunk.text:
What is respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)? 
 Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, is a common respiratory virus. It usually causes mild, cold-like symptoms. But it can cause serious lung infections, especially in infants, older adults, and people with serious medical problems. 

 How is respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) spread? 
 RSV spreads from person to person through: 
 The air by coughing and sneezing 
 Direct contact, such as kissing the face of a child who has RSV 
 Touching an object or surface with the virus on it, then touching your mouth, nose, or eyes before washing your hands 
 
 People who have an RSV infection are usually contagious for 3 to 8 days. But sometimes infants and people with weakened immune systems can continue to spread the virus for as long as 4 weeks. 

 Who is at risk for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections? 
 RSV can affect people of all ages. But it is very common in small children; nearly all children become infected with RSV by age 2. In the United States, RSV infections usually occur during RSV season, which is usually fall through spring. 

 Certain people are at higher risk of having a severe RSV infection: 
 Infants 
 Older adults, especially those ages 65 and older 
 People with chronic medical conditions such as heart or lung disease 
 People with weakened immune systems 
 
 What are the symptoms of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections? 
 The symptoms of RSV infection usually start about 4 to 6 days after infection. They include: 
 Runny nose 
 Decrease in appetite 
 Cough 
 Sneezing 
 Fever 
 Wheezing 
 
 These symptoms usually appear in stages instead of all at once. In very young infants, the only symptoms may be irritability, decreased activity, and trouble breathing.

**Cardinal sign: stridor**
- Inspiratory stridor = supraglottic or glottic obstruction
- Biphasic stridor = subglottic obstruction (tracheal)
- Expiratory stridor = intrathoracic tracheal/bronchial obstruction
- ABSENCE of stridor with severe distress = near-complete obstruction or exhaustion

**Clinical assessment:**
- Tripod positioning, drooling, voice changes (muffled "hot potato voice")
- Difficulty swallowing secretions
- Intercostal/suprasternal retractions, accessory muscle use
- Cyanosis, agitation → somnolence (impending arrest)
- Universal choking sign (hands at throat) — foreign body

**Common etiologies:**
- **Foreign body aspiration** — sudden onset during eating or play, choking episode
- **Angioedema** — lip/tongue/uvula swelling; histamine-mediated (allergic) or bradykinin-mediated (ACE inhibitor, hereditary)
- **Epiglottitis** — fever, severe sore throat, drooling, "hot potato" voice, rapid onset (now increasingly adults > children post-Hib vaccine)
- **Peritonsillar abscess** — unilateral tonsillar swelling, trismus, uvular deviation, muffled voice
- **Retropharyngeal abscess** — neck stiffness, dysphagia, posterior pharyngeal swelling, fever (CT diagnostic)
- **Ludwig angina** — floor of mouth cellulitis, submandibular swelling, tongue elevation, dental source
- **Anaphylaxis** — laryngeal edema component; urticaria, hypotension, bronchospasm
- **Burns/inhalation injury** — singed nasal hairs, soot in oropharynx, hoarseness, history of fire/smoke exposure
- **Tumor** — gradual onset, progressive

 These symptoms usually appear in stages instead of all at once. In very young infants, the only symptoms may be irritability, decreased activity, and trouble breathing. 
 RSV can also cause more severe infections, especially in people at high risk. These infections include bronchiolitis, an inflammation of the small airways in the lung, and pneumonia , an infection of the lungs. 

 How are respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections diagnosed? 
 Your health care provider may use many tools to make a diagnosis: 
 A medical history, including asking about symptoms. 
 A physical exam. 
 A lab test of nasal fluid or another respiratory specimen to check for RSV. This is usually done for people with severe infection. 
 Tests to check for complications in people with severe infection. The tests may include a chest x-ray and blood and urine tests. 
 
 What are the treatments for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections? 
 There is no specific treatment for RSV infection. Most infections go away on their own in a week or two. Over-the-counter pain relievers can help with the fever and pain. However, do not give aspirin to children. And do not give cough medicine to children under four. It is also important to get enough fluids to prevent dehydration . 

 Some people with severe infection may need to be hospitalized. There, they might get oxygen , a breathing tube, or a ventilator. 

 Can respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections be prevented? 
 There are some vaccines to protect against RSV illness. Two of them are for people ages 60 and older. If you are in this age group, talk to your provider about whether an RSV vaccine would be right for you.

**Definition:** Rapidly progressive inflammation of the epiglottis and surrounding supraglottic structures, causing airway obstruction. Now predominantly an adult disease in the post-Hib vaccine era.

### Classic Presentation
- Severe sore throat disproportionate to pharyngeal findings
- Dysphagia, odynophagia, drooling
- Muffled "hot potato" voice
- Stridor (late and ominous — indicates >50% airway narrowing)
- Tripod positioning, neck extension ("sniffing position")
- Rapid onset (hours, not days)
- Fever, toxic appearance

### Adult vs Pediatric Differences
| Feature | Pediatric (rare post-vaccine) | Adult |
|---|---|---|
| Onset | Fulminant (hours) | Subacute possible (12-24 hours) |
| Drooling | Common | Less common |
| Airway obstruction | Rapid, higher risk | Variable, still dangerous |
| Etiology | H. influenzae type B (if unvaccinated) | Polymicrobial; Strep, Staph, H. influenzae non-typeable |
| Thumbprint sign | Classic | Present in 60-80% |

### Red Flags for Imminent Airway Loss
- Stridor at rest
- Inability to swallow secretions
- Sitting upright, refusing to lie down
- Cyanosis
- Altered mental status
- Rapid clinical deterioration

chunk.text:
1. **Ordering unnecessary viral testing.** RSV or respiratory viral panel results do not change management for individual patients. Positive tests lead to parental anxiety and do not guide therapy. Negative tests do not exclude bronchiolitis (clinical diagnosis). Viral testing is only useful for cohorting inpatients during RSV season, not for ED decision-making.

2. **Obtaining a chest X-ray in uncomplicated bronchiolitis.** CXR findings in bronchiolitis (atelectasis, peribronchial cuffing, hyperinflation) are frequently misinterpreted as bacterial pneumonia, leading to inappropriate antibiotic prescriptions in up to 25-30% of cases where CXR is obtained. Reserve imaging for atypical presentations, clinical deterioration, or ICU-level disease.

3. **Administering albuterol or corticosteroids.** Despite strong AAP recommendations against their use, bronchodilators and systemic steroids remain widely prescribed for bronchiolitis. Neither agent has demonstrated benefit in RCTs. A "trial of albuterol" is particularly misleading: any apparent improvement is likely from nasal suctioning performed concurrently, spontaneous fluctuation, or placebo effect. Ordering these medications delays recognition that supportive care is the only effective treatment.

4. **Prescribing antibiotics without evidence of bacterial co-infection.** Concurrent serious bacterial infection in bronchiolitis is rare (UTI ~1-2% in febrile infants; bacteremia < 1%). Antibiotics are not indicated unless a specific bacterial infection is documented (positive urine culture, lobar consolidation with high fever, toxic appearance). The viral illness itself causes fever and elevated inflammatory markers, which should not be misinterpreted as bacterial infection.

chunk.text:
1. **Forcing the patient supine for examination or imaging.** Supine positioning collapses the already compromised airway. Examine and image with the patient sitting upright.

2. **Performing blind oropharyngeal exam with a tongue depressor.** Direct oropharyngeal manipulation triggers laryngospasm and complete airway obstruction. Use flexible nasopharyngoscopy in a controlled setting.

3. **Delaying ENT/anesthesia notification because the patient "looks stable."** Epiglottitis deteriorates unpredictably. Dual specialty notification (ENT + anesthesia) happens at time of suspicion, not after confirmation.

4. **Anchoring on the classic pediatric presentation in adults.** Adult epiglottitis presents with severe sore throat and dysphagia more than stridor and drooling. A severe sore throat with a relatively normal oropharyngeal exam demands further evaluation.

5. **Attempting ED intubation in a semi-stable patient.** OR intubation with fiber-optic guidance, ENT backup, and surgical airway readiness is the standard. ED intubation is reserved for complete airway loss.

6. **Discharging as "pharyngitis" without visualizing the epiglottis.** The oropharynx appears deceptively normal in epiglottitis — the pathology is supraglottic. Severe sore throat with pain out of proportion to exam findings warrants lateral neck X-ray or nasopharyngoscopy.

7. **Omitting MRSA coverage in critically ill patients.** Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus causes epiglottitis, particularly in immunocompromised patients and those with healthcare exposure. Add vancomycin in severe cases.

8. **Relying on a normal lateral neck X-ray to exclude epiglottitis.** Sensitivity is only 79-88%. A negative X-ray in a patient with high clinical suspicion requires direct visualization or CT.

sources.text:
What is respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)? 
 Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, is a common respiratory virus. It usually causes mild, cold-like symptoms. But it can cause serious lung infections, especially in infants, older adults, and people with serious medical problems. 

 How is respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) spread? 
 RSV spreads from person to person through: 
 The air by coughing and sneezing 
 Direct contact, such as kissing the face of a child who has RSV 
 Touching an object or surface with the virus on it, then touching your mouth, nose, or eyes before washing your hands 
 
 People who have an RSV infection are usually contagious for 3 to 8 days. But sometimes infants and people with weakened immune systems can continue to spread the virus for as long as 4 weeks. 

 Who is at risk for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections? 
 RSV can affect people of all ages. But it is very common in small children; nearly all children become infected with RSV by age 2. In the United States, RSV infections usually occur during RSV season, which is usually fall through spring. 

 Certain people are at higher risk of having a severe RSV infection: 
 Infants 
 Older adults, especially those ages 65 and older 
 People with chronic medical conditions such as heart or lung disease 
 People with weakened immune systems 
 
 What are the symptoms of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections? 
 The symptoms of RSV infection usually start about 4 to 6 days after infection. They include: 
 Runny nose 
 Decrease in appetite 
 Cough 
 Sneezing 
 Fever 
 Wheezing 
 
 These symptoms usually appear in stages instead of all at once. In very young infants, the only symptoms may be irritability, decreased activity, and trouble breathing.

sources.text:
**Cardinal sign: stridor**
- Inspiratory stridor = supraglottic or glottic obstruction
- Biphasic stridor = subglottic obstruction (tracheal)
- Expiratory stridor = intrathoracic tracheal/bronchial obstruction
- ABSENCE of stridor with severe distress = near-complete obstruction or exhaustion

**Clinical assessment:**
- Tripod positioning, drooling, voice changes (muffled "hot potato voice")
- Difficulty swallowing secretions
- Intercostal/suprasternal retractions, accessory muscle use
- Cyanosis, agitation → somnolence (impending arrest)
- Universal choking sign (hands at throat) — foreign body

**Common etiologies:**
- **Foreign body aspiration** — sudden onset during eating or play, choking episode
- **Angioedema** — lip/tongue/uvula swelling; histamine-mediated (allergic) or bradykinin-mediated (ACE inhibitor, hereditary)
- **Epiglottitis** — fever, severe sore throat, drooling, "hot potato" voice, rapid onset (now increasingly adults > children post-Hib vaccine)
- **Peritonsillar abscess** — unilateral tonsillar swelling, trismus, uvular deviation, muffled voice
- **Retropharyngeal abscess** — neck stiffness, dysphagia, posterior pharyngeal swelling, fever (CT diagnostic)
- **Ludwig angina** — floor of mouth cellulitis, submandibular swelling, tongue elevation, dental source
- **Anaphylaxis** — laryngeal edema component; urticaria, hypotension, bronchospasm
- **Burns/inhalation injury** — singed nasal hairs, soot in oropharynx, hoarseness, history of fire/smoke exposure
- **Tumor** — gradual onset, progressive

 How are respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections diagnosed? 
 Your health care provider may use many tools to make a diagnosis: 
 A medical history, including asking about symptoms. 
 A physical exam. 
 A lab test of nasal fluid or another respiratory specimen to check for RSV. This is usually done for people with severe infection. 
 Tests to check for complications in people with severe infection. The tests may include a chest x-ray and blood and urine tests. 
 
 What are the treatments for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections? 
 There is no specific treatment for RSV infection. Most infections go away on their own in a week or two. Over-the-counter pain relievers can help with the fever and pain. However, do not give aspirin to children. And do not give cough medicine to children under four. It is also important to get enough fluids to prevent dehydration . 

 Some people with severe infection may need to be hospitalized. There, they might get oxygen , a breathing tube, or a ventilator. 

 Can respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections be prevented? 
 There are some vaccines to protect against RSV illness. Two of them are for people ages 60 and older. If you are in this age group, talk to your provider about whether an RSV vaccine would be right for you.

sources.text:
**Definition:** Rapidly progressive inflammation of the epiglottis and surrounding supraglottic structures, causing airway obstruction. Now predominantly an adult disease in the post-Hib vaccine era.

### Classic Presentation
- Severe sore throat disproportionate to pharyngeal findings
- Dysphagia, odynophagia, drooling
- Muffled "hot potato" voice
- Stridor (late and ominous — indicates >50% airway narrowing)
- Tripod positioning, neck extension ("sniffing position")
- Rapid onset (hours, not days)
- Fever, toxic appearance

### Adult vs Pediatric Differences
| Feature | Pediatric (rare post-vaccine) | Adult |
|---|---|---|
| Onset | Fulminant (hours) | Subacute possible (12-24 hours) |
| Drooling | Common | Less common |
| Airway obstruction | Rapid, higher risk | Variable, still dangerous |
| Etiology | H. influenzae type B (if unvaccinated) | Polymicrobial; Strep, Staph, H. influenzae non-typeable |
| Thumbprint sign | Classic | Present in 60-80% |

### Red Flags for Imminent Airway Loss
- Stridor at rest
- Inability to swallow secretions
- Sitting upright, refusing to lie down
- Cyanosis
- Altered mental status
- Rapid clinical deterioration

quoteSpans.text: What is respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)?
Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, is a common respiratory virus.
It usually causes mild, cold-like symptoms.
But it can cause serious lung infections, especially in infants, older adults, and people with serious medical problems.
How is respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) spread?
RSV spreads from person to person through:
The air by coughing and sneezing
Direct contact, such as kissing the face of a child who has RSV
Touching an object or surface with the virus on it, then touching your mouth, nose, or eyes before washing your hands
People who have an RSV infection are usually contagious for 3 to 8 days.
But sometimes infants and people with weakened immune systems can continue to spread the virus for as long as 4 weeks.
Who is at risk for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections?
RSV can affect people of all ages.
But it is very common in small children; nearly all children become infected with RSV by age 2.
In the United States, RSV infections usually occur during RSV season, which is usually fall through spring.
Certain people are at higher risk of having a severe RSV infection:
Infants
Older adults, especially those ages 65 and older
People with chronic medical conditions such as heart or lung disease
People with weakened immune systems
What are the symptoms of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections?
The symptoms of RSV infection usually start about 4 to 6 days after infection.
They include:
Runny nose
Decrease in appetite
Cough
Sneezing
Fever
Wheezing
These symptoms usually appear in stages instead of all at once.
In very young infants, the only symptoms may be irritability, decreased activity, and trouble breathing.

quoteSpans.text: **Cardinal sign: stridor**

- Biphasic stridor = subglottic obstruction (tracheal)

- Tripod positioning, drooling, voice changes (muffled "hot potato voice")
- Difficulty swallowing secretions
- Intercostal/suprasternal retractions, accessory muscle use
- Cyanosis, agitation → somnolence (impending arrest)

- **Foreign body aspiration** — sudden onset during eating or play, choking episode

How are respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections diagnosed?
Your health care provider may use many tools to make a diagnosis:
A medical history, including asking about symptoms.
A physical exam.
A lab test of nasal fluid or another respiratory specimen to check for RSV.
This is usually done for people with severe infection.
Tests to check for complications in people with severe infection.

What are the treatments for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections?
There is no specific treatment for RSV infection.
Most infections go away on their own in a week or two.
Over-the-counter pain relievers can help with the fever and pain.
However, do not give aspirin to children.
And do not give cough medicine to children under four.
It is also important to get enough fluids to prevent dehydration .
Some people with severe infection may need to be hospitalized.
There, they might get oxygen , a breathing tube, or a ventilator.
Can respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections be prevented?
There are some vaccines to protect against RSV illness.
Two of them are for people ages 60 and older.
If you are in this age group, talk to your provider about whether an RSV vaccine would be right for you.

quoteSpans.text: **Definition:** Rapidly progressive inflammation of the epiglottis and surrounding supraglottic structures, causing airway obstruction.
Now predominantly an adult disease in the post-Hib vaccine era.
### Classic Presentation
- Severe sore throat disproportionate to pharyngeal findings
- Dysphagia, odynophagia, drooling
- Muffled "hot potato" voice
- Stridor (late and ominous — indicates >50% airway narrowing)
- Tripod positioning, neck extension ("sniffing position")
- Rapid onset (hours, not days)
- Fever, toxic appearance
### Adult vs Pediatric Differences
| Feature | Pediatric (rare post-vaccine) | Adult |
| Onset | Fulminant (hours) | Subacute possible (12-24 hours) |
| Drooling | Common | Less common |
| Airway obstruction | Rapid, higher risk | Variable, still dangerous |
| Etiology | H. influenzae type B (if unvaccinated) | Polymicrobial; Strep, Staph, H. influenzae non-typeable |
| Thumbprint sign | Classic | Present in 60-80% |
### Red Flags for Imminent Airway Loss
- Stridor at rest
- Inability to swallow secretions
- Sitting upright, refusing to lie down
- Cyanosis
- Altered mental status
- Rapid clinical deterioration

quoteSpans.text: **Ordering unnecessary viral testing.
** RSV or respiratory viral panel results do not change management for individual patients.
Positive tests lead to parental anxiety and do not guide therapy.
Negative tests do not exclude bronchiolitis (clinical diagnosis).
Viral testing is only useful for cohorting inpatients during RSV season, not for ED decision-making.
**Obtaining a chest X-ray in uncomplicated bronchiolitis.

** CXR findings in bronchiolitis (atelectasis, peribronchial cuffing, hyperinflation) are frequently misinterpreted as bacterial pneumonia, leading to inappropriate antibiotic prescriptions in up to 25-30% of cases where CXR is obtained.
Reserve imaging for atypical presentations, clinical deterioration, or ICU-level disease.
**Administering albuterol or corticosteroids.
** Despite strong AAP recommendations against their use, bronchodilators and systemic steroids remain widely prescribed for bronchiolitis.
Neither agent has demonstrated benefit in RCTs.
A "trial of albuterol" is particularly misleading: any apparent improvement is likely from nasal suctioning performed concurrently, spontaneous fluctuation, or placebo effect.
Ordering these medications delays recognition that supportive care is the only effective treatment.
**Prescribing antibiotics without evidence of bacterial co-infection.
** Concurrent serious bacterial infection in bronchiolitis is rare (UTI ~1-2% in febrile infants; bacteremia < 1%).
Antibiotics are not indicated unless a specific bacterial infection is documented (positive urine culture, lobar consolidation with high fever, toxic appearance).
The viral illness itself causes fever and elevated inflammatory markers, which should not be misinterpreted as bacterial infection.

quoteSpans.text: **Forcing the patient supine for examination or imaging.
** Supine positioning collapses the already compromised airway.
Examine and image with the patient sitting upright.
**Performing blind oropharyngeal exam with a tongue depressor.
** Direct oropharyngeal manipulation triggers laryngospasm and complete airway obstruction.
Use flexible nasopharyngoscopy in a controlled setting.
**Delaying ENT/anesthesia notification because the patient "looks stable."
** Epiglottitis deteriorates unpredictably.
Dual specialty notification (ENT + anesthesia) happens at time of suspicion, not after confirmation.
**Anchoring on the classic pediatric presentation in adults.
** Adult epiglottitis presents with severe sore throat and dysphagia more than stridor and drooling.
A severe sore throat with a relatively normal oropharyngeal exam demands further evaluation.
**Attempting ED intubation in a semi-stable patient.
** OR intubation with fiber-optic guidance, ENT backup, and surgical airway readiness is the standard.
ED intubation is reserved for complete airway loss.
**Discharging as "pharyngitis" without visualizing the epiglottis.
** The oropharynx appears deceptively normal in epiglottitis — the pathology is supraglottic.
Severe sore throat with pain out of proportion to exam findings warrants lateral neck X-ray or nasopharyngoscopy.
**Omitting MRSA coverage in critically ill patients.
** Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus causes epiglottitis, particularly in immunocompromised patients and those with healthcare exposure.
Add vancomycin in severe cases.
**Relying on a normal lateral neck X-ray to exclude epiglottitis.
** Sensitivity is only 79-88%.
A negative X-ray in a patient with high clinical suspicion requires direct visualization or CT.

- **Roseola (HHV-6):** fever × 3-5 days, then diffuse maculopapular rash as fever resolves. Benign.
- **Viral gastroenteritis:** fever, vomiting, diarrhea. Assess hydration status.

What is respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)? 
 Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, is a common respiratory virus. It usually causes mild, cold-like symptoms. But it can cause serious lung infections, especially in infants, older adults, and people with serious medical problems. 

 How is respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) spread? 
 RSV spreads from person to person through: 
 The air by coughing and sneezing 
 Direct contact, such as kissing the face of a child who has RSV 
 Touching an object or surface with the virus on it, then touching your mouth, nose, or eyes before washing your hands 
 
 People who have an RSV infection are usually contagious for 3 to 8 days. But sometimes infants and people with weakened immune systems can continue to spread the virus for as long as 4 weeks. 

 Who is at risk for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections? 
 RSV can affect people of all ages. But it is very common in small children; nearly all children become infected with RSV by age 2. In the United States, RSV infections usually occur during RSV season, which is usually fall through spring. 

 Certain people are at higher risk of having a severe RSV infection: 
 Infants 
 Older adults, especially those ages 65 and older 
 People with chronic medical conditions such as heart or lung disease 
 People with weakened immune systems 
 
 What are the symptoms of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections? 
 The symptoms of RSV infection usually start about 4 to 6 days after infection. They include: 
 Runny nose 
 Decrease in appetite 
 Cough 
 Sneezing 
 Fever 
 Wheezing 
 
 These symptoms usually appear in stages instead of all at once. In very young infants, the only symptoms may be irritability, decreased activity, and trouble breathing.

**Cardinal sign: stridor**
- Inspiratory stridor = supraglottic or glottic obstruction
- Biphasic stridor = subglottic obstruction (tracheal)
- Expiratory stridor = intrathoracic tracheal/bronchial obstruction
- ABSENCE of stridor with severe distress = near-complete obstruction or exhaustion

**Clinical assessment:**
- Tripod positioning, drooling, voice changes (muffled "hot potato voice")
- Difficulty swallowing secretions
- Intercostal/suprasternal retractions, accessory muscle use
- Cyanosis, agitation → somnolence (impending arrest)
- Universal choking sign (hands at throat) — foreign body

**Common etiologies:**
- **Foreign body aspiration** — sudden onset during eating or play, choking episode
- **Angioedema** — lip/tongue/uvula swelling; histamine-mediated (allergic) or bradykinin-mediated (ACE inhibitor, hereditary)
- **Epiglottitis** — fever, severe sore throat, drooling, "hot potato" voice, rapid onset (now increasingly adults > children post-Hib vaccine)
- **Peritonsillar abscess** — unilateral tonsillar swelling, trismus, uvular deviation, muffled voice
- **Retropharyngeal abscess** — neck stiffness, dysphagia, posterior pharyngeal swelling, fever (CT diagnostic)
- **Ludwig angina** — floor of mouth cellulitis, submandibular swelling, tongue elevation, dental source
- **Anaphylaxis** — laryngeal edema component; urticaria, hypotension, bronchospasm
- **Burns/inhalation injury** — singed nasal hairs, soot in oropharynx, hoarseness, history of fire/smoke exposure
- **Tumor** — gradual onset, progressive

 RSV can also cause more severe infections, especially in people at high risk. These infections include bronchiolitis, an inflammation of the small airways in the lung, and pneumonia , an infection of the lungs. 

 How are respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections diagnosed? 
 Your health care provider may use many tools to make a diagnosis: 
 A medical history, including asking about symptoms. 
 A physical exam. 
 A lab test of nasal fluid or another respiratory specimen to check for RSV. This is usually done for people with severe infection. 
 Tests to check for complications in people with severe infection. The tests may include a chest x-ray and blood and urine tests. 
 
 What are the treatments for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections? 
 There is no specific treatment for RSV infection. Most infections go away on their own in a week or two. Over-the-counter pain relievers can help with the fever and pain. However, do not give aspirin to children. And do not give cough medicine to children under four. It is also important to get enough fluids to prevent dehydration . 

 Some people with severe infection may need to be hospitalized. There, they might get oxygen , a breathing tube, or a ventilator. 

 Can respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections be prevented? 
 There are some vaccines to protect against RSV illness. Two of them are for people ages 60 and older. If you are in this age group, talk to your provider about whether an RSV vaccine would be right for you.

**Definition:** Rapidly progressive inflammation of the epiglottis and surrounding supraglottic structures, causing airway obstruction. Now predominantly an adult disease in the post-Hib vaccine era.

### Classic Presentation
- Severe sore throat disproportionate to pharyngeal findings
- Dysphagia, odynophagia, drooling
- Muffled "hot potato" voice
- Stridor (late and ominous — indicates >50% airway narrowing)
- Tripod positioning, neck extension ("sniffing position")
- Rapid onset (hours, not days)
- Fever, toxic appearance

### Adult vs Pediatric Differences
| Feature | Pediatric (rare post-vaccine) | Adult |
|---|---|---|
| Onset | Fulminant (hours) | Subacute possible (12-24 hours) |
| Drooling | Common | Less common |
| Airway obstruction | Rapid, higher risk | Variable, still dangerous |
| Etiology | H. influenzae type B (if unvaccinated) | Polymicrobial; Strep, Staph, H. influenzae non-typeable |
| Thumbprint sign | Classic | Present in 60-80% |

### Red Flags for Imminent Airway Loss
- Stridor at rest
- Inability to swallow secretions
- Sitting upright, refusing to lie down
- Cyanosis
- Altered mental status
- Rapid clinical deterioration

1. **Ordering unnecessary viral testing.** RSV or respiratory viral panel results do not change management for individual patients. Positive tests lead to parental anxiety and do not guide therapy. Negative tests do not exclude bronchiolitis (clinical diagnosis). Viral testing is only useful for cohorting inpatients during RSV season, not for ED decision-making.

2. **Obtaining a chest X-ray in uncomplicated bronchiolitis.** CXR findings in bronchiolitis (atelectasis, peribronchial cuffing, hyperinflation) are frequently misinterpreted as bacterial pneumonia, leading to inappropriate antibiotic prescriptions in up to 25-30% of cases where CXR is obtained. Reserve imaging for atypical presentations, clinical deterioration, or ICU-level disease.

3. **Administering albuterol or corticosteroids.** Despite strong AAP recommendations against their use, bronchodilators and systemic steroids remain widely prescribed for bronchiolitis. Neither agent has demonstrated benefit in RCTs. A "trial of albuterol" is particularly misleading: any apparent improvement is likely from nasal suctioning performed concurrently, spontaneous fluctuation, or placebo effect. Ordering these medications delays recognition that supportive care is the only effective treatment.

4. **Prescribing antibiotics without evidence of bacterial co-infection.** Concurrent serious bacterial infection in bronchiolitis is rare (UTI ~1-2% in febrile infants; bacteremia < 1%). Antibiotics are not indicated unless a specific bacterial infection is documented (positive urine culture, lobar consolidation with high fever, toxic appearance). The viral illness itself causes fever and elevated inflammatory markers, which should not be misinterpreted as bacterial infection.

1. **Forcing the patient supine for examination or imaging.** Supine positioning collapses the already compromised airway. Examine and image with the patient sitting upright.

2. **Performing blind oropharyngeal exam with a tongue depressor.** Direct oropharyngeal manipulation triggers laryngospasm and complete airway obstruction. Use flexible nasopharyngoscopy in a controlled setting.

3. **Delaying ENT/anesthesia notification because the patient "looks stable."** Epiglottitis deteriorates unpredictably. Dual specialty notification (ENT + anesthesia) happens at time of suspicion, not after confirmation.

4. **Anchoring on the classic pediatric presentation in adults.** Adult epiglottitis presents with severe sore throat and dysphagia more than stridor and drooling. A severe sore throat with a relatively normal oropharyngeal exam demands further evaluation.

5. **Attempting ED intubation in a semi-stable patient.** OR intubation with fiber-optic guidance, ENT backup, and surgical airway readiness is the standard. ED intubation is reserved for complete airway loss.

6. **Discharging as "pharyngitis" without visualizing the epiglottis.** The oropharynx appears deceptively normal in epiglottitis — the pathology is supraglottic. Severe sore throat with pain out of proportion to exam findings warrants lateral neck X-ray or nasopharyngoscopy.

7. **Omitting MRSA coverage in critically ill patients.** Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus causes epiglottitis, particularly in immunocompromised patients and those with healthcare exposure. Add vancomycin in severe cases.

8. **Relying on a normal lateral neck X-ray to exclude epiglottitis.** Sensitivity is only 79-88%. A negative X-ray in a patient with high clinical suspicion requires direct visualization or CT.
